title: Dr. Heidegger's Experiment
focus: the foolishness of wishing to be young again

teacherSummary.text: Old Dr. Heidegger invites four elderly friends, each ruined by vice, to test water from the Fountain of Youth. A withered rose revives in it. The guests drink, grow young, and repeat their old follies: flirting with the widow Wycherly and fighting over her until they knock the vase to the floor. The effect wears off; the rose withers. The doctor has learned his lesson, but the guests resolve to go to Florida to drink from the fountain.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Dr. Heidegger's Experiment,” how does Hawthorne show the foolishness of wishing to be young again? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Dr. Heidegger's Experiment, how does Hawthorne develop the idea of the foolishness of wishing to be young again? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Dr. Heidegger's Experiment develops the idea of the foolishness of wishing to be young again. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Dr. Heidegger's Experiment (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of the foolishness of wishing to be young again. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Dr. Heidegger's Experiment suggests about the foolishness of wishing to be young again. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's irony and symbolism), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Nathaniel Hawthorne uses irony in Dr. Heidegger's Experiment to complicate the reader's understanding of the foolishness of wishing to be young again. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Dr. Heidegger's Experiment within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of the foolishness of wishing to be young again responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Dr. Heidegger's Experiment alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of the foolishness of wishing to be young again follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Dr. Heidegger's Experiment and its treatment of the foolishness of wishing to be young again. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's irony and symbolism, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Dr. Heidegger's Experiment as evidence for a larger claim about the foolishness of wishing to be young again in Dr. Heidegger's Experiment. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Dr. Heidegger's Experiment as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of the foolishness of wishing to be young again. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Dr. Heidegger's Experiment.

satQuestions.passage: 'This rose,' said Dr. Heidegger, with a sigh, 'this same withered and crumbling flower, blossomed five-and-fifty years ago. It was given me by Sylvia Ward, whose portrait hangs yonder; and I meant to wear it in my bosom at our wedding. Five-and-fifty years it has been treasured between the leaves of this old volume. Now, would you deem it possible that this rose of half a century could ever bloom again?'

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: If you could be ten years older or younger for a day, what would you do differently? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: Nothing in this story needs a special warning.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are exuberant, blossomed, interchange, scandalous, gentlewoman. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “They were a group of merry youngsters, almost maddened with the exuberant frolicksomeness of their years.” In this sentence it means: joyously unrestrained. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Dr. Heidegger's Experiment would have known. Collected in Twice-Told Tales (1837); Ponce de León's legendary search in Florida is the allusion. Why does this story matter? A tidy moral tale often paired with discussion of whether people learn from experience. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for irony.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “'This rose,' said Dr.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the foolishness of wishing to be young again? I circle “blossomed”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find irony, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of irony. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: 'This rose,' said Dr. Heidegger, with a sigh, 'this same withered and crumbling flower, blossomed five-and-fifty years ago. It was given me by Sylvia Ward, whose portrait hangs yonder; and I meant to wear it in my bosom at our wedding. Five-and-fifty years it has been treasured between the leaves of this old volume. Now, would you deem it possible that this rose of half a century could ever bloom again?'

Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Dr. Heidegger's Experiment develops the idea of the foolishness of wishing to be young again. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this story connect to youth and folly? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Story quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the story quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this story suggests about the foolishness of wishing to be young again, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how irony shapes the foolishness of wishing to be young again. Tonight, read the next story and add two words to your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
